newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Strike takes Venezuelan health system to the brink.
newsitem.headline: Strike takes Venezuelan health system to the brink.

text.p: Venezuelan authorities, trying to end a week-old public doctors' strike, said on Friday an investigation had been ordered in the deaths of 10 patients who died for apparent lack of adequate medical care.
National Public Prosecutor Ivan Dario Badell told reporters some of the 10 reported cases could be of "homicide by negligence ... as stated in the penal code" and threatened legal action.

Union delegates of Venezuela's 25,000 public doctors, who are demanding a substantial pay increase, blamed the government's intransigence for health hazards arising at some of the country's 380 public hospitals and 6,000 clinics.
At emergency wards mostly staffed by military doctors and medical students nationwide, chaos sometimes prevailed. Women about to give birth faced agonizingly long waits.

Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff, often acting as the government's unofficial spokesman, on Friday reiterated the government's unwillingness to negotiate with the striking doctors, saying "all in Venezuela repudiated their action."
"The government is willing to negotiate if work resumes in emergency wards. Its proposal remains a 25 percent wage increase," he told reporters after the weekly cabinet meeting.
Venezuelan doctors, who earn a minimum $126 per month and a $304 monthly average including bonuses, said they lag far behind their colleagues in other Latin American countries.
After asking for a $1,000 minimum salary, the Federation of Venezuelan Doctors (FMV) said it would settle for $735.
"We've been discussing this (salary) problem with the government for the past 14 months. We're being denied decent wages," FMV executive committee member Juan Bautista Diaz said.
Doctors say the Health Ministry's budget is too small and has left hospitals without proper equipment and supplies as basic as needles and gauze.
At Caracas Concepcion Palacios main maternity, women gave birth on Friday sometimes with only the help of nurses.

"Doctors can't do this," lamented Carmen, 21, from a poor neighborhood near Caracas as she sat in the emergency room. About 30 other women, some obviously in pain, were there waiting to deliver their babies.
